title: INNER JOIN Deep Dive
description: Combine matching records across multiple tables with ANSI SQL-92 INNER JOIN, join filters, and multi-table relationships.

data.text: **`INNER JOIN`** returns rows when there is a match in both the left and right tables. If a row in Table A does not match any row in Table B according to the join condition, it is omitted from the result set.

data.title: Joining Customers, Orders, and Order Items
data.content: Combining three tables using clean table aliases.
data.code:
SELECT 
    c.id AS customer_id,
    c.name AS customer_name,
    o.id AS order_id,
    o.ordered_at,
    p.title AS product_name,
    oi.quantity,
    oi.unit_price
FROM customers c
INNER JOIN orders o 
    ON o.customer_id = c.id
INNER JOIN order_items oi 
    ON oi.order_id = o.id
INNER JOIN products p 
    ON p.id = oi.product_id
WHERE o.status = 'COMPLETED'
ORDER BY o.ordered_at DESC
LIMIT 50;

data.title: ON vs WHERE in INNER JOINs
data.text: In an `INNER JOIN`, placing non-join filters in the `ON` clause versus the `WHERE` clause produces identical results. However, putting join predicates in `ON` and filtering predicates in `WHERE` makes your SQL vastly more readable.

An INNER JOIN between a parent and multiple children multiplies the parent row. Joining orders to order items is correct, but joining orders to both order items and shipments in the same query double-counts money. The fix is to aggregate each child in a subquery first, then join the smaller result sets to the parent.

data.title: Aggregate before joining to avoid double counting
data.content: Each child table is reduced to one row per order, so the final join cannot fan out.
data.code:
SELECT
    o.id,
    o.ordered_at,
    i.item_total,
    s.shipped_total
FROM orders AS o
INNER JOIN (
    SELECT order_id, SUM(quantity * unit_price) AS item_total
    FROM order_items
    GROUP BY order_id
) AS i
    ON i.order_id = o.id
LEFT JOIN (
    SELECT order_id, SUM(cost) AS shipped_total
    FROM shipments
    GROUP BY order_id
) AS s
    ON s.order_id = o.id
WHERE o.status = 'COMPLETED'
ORDER BY o.ordered_at DESC;

data.title: Interview angle: cardinality before syntax
data.text: When asked to join several tables, first say how many rows each relationship can produce: one-to-one, one-to-many, or many-to-many. Interviewers listen for whether you check cardinality before writing the join, because that is what prevents inflated totals in production. Mention `EXPLAIN` and row-count checks as your verification tools.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: `INNER JOIN` excludes non-matching rows from both tables.
Always use clear table aliases (`c`, `o`, `oi`) for readability.
Chain multiple joins sequentially to traverse relational paths.
